summary: AE + SE from Redwood scoped a POC with AetherEdge to validate capacity sizing and autoscaling strategy. Customer wants reserved GPUs for baseline throughput with burst capacity for spiky workloads, and explicit fallback policies to cheaper model variants or region-level failover. Success criteria include p95 latency <= 250ms for 512 tokens, sub-$X cost per 1M tokens, and throughput of 200 concurrent requests across several models. Next steps: sizing workbook, benchmark run, and proposal with pricing and contract terms.
topics: workload sizing: qps, concurrency, model types
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we will record. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Carlos is our SE. Could folks introduce quickly?
[00:12] Jared Kim: Jared here, CTO at AetherEdge. Lina is head of MLOps and Samir leads infra.
[00:20] Lina Zhao: hi, hi, thanks for doing this.
[00:24] Carlos Ortega: Yeah hi all, quick agenda - we want to align on POC success criteria, sizing, and how we'll handle reserved GPUs and burst autoscale, plus fallback strategies.
[00:36] Samir Patel: Sounds good. Our main thing is predictable latency under load, we also need cost guardrails.
[00:44] Maya Patel: Perfect, ok quick Q: what's your expected baseline qps and peak?
[00:50] Jared Kim: Baseline around 40 qps, peaks up to 350 qps in spikes, but spikes are short, 30-60s bursts. It's mostly chat completions and a rerank service.
[01:05] Lina Zhao: models are two families: a 7B-ish chat model for UI and a 20B reranker for search. We'll share exact model names, might be a mix of open models.
[01:15] Carlos Ortega: Got it. For conversation - are you targeting 512 tokens typical or longer?
[01:22] Samir Patel: median 128, tail to 1024. For rerank it's short - 64 tokens.
[01:29] Maya Patel: Thanks. For POC success criteria - from our checklist: latency p95 target, cost per 1M tokens or per inference, error rate, and sustained throughput. Any additions?
[01:40] Jared Kim: Also fallbacks - if reserved capacity saturated, we need automated fallback to either smaller quantized variant or alternate region.
[01:49] Lina Zhao: And audit logs/SSO are required but that's a separate security doc we asked for.
[01:55] Carlos Ortega: Noted. We'll include fallback patterns and security attachments.
[02:00] Speaker 1: [inaudible]
[02:08] Carlos Ortega: Ok on capacity - recommended POC baseline is reserved GPUs sized to handle 95% of baseline traffic with headroom. So if baseline is 40 qps we size for like 60 qps reserve and rely on burst pool for spikes.
[02:22] Samir Patel: When you say "burst pool" what's the cold start behavior? we can't have big latency hits.
[02:28] Carlos Ortega: Good call, bursts are pre-warmed instances with low-concurrency slots or fast-start kernels. There's a tradeoff: keeping a hot standby increases cost. For 30-60s spikes we recommend a small prewarmed cushion plus fast scaling on GPU-backed nodes.
[02:44] Maya Patel: And we can configure maximum cold-start latency - e.g., allow up to 500ms additional for initial token as a policy. Does that work?
[02:52] Lina Zhao: 500ms extra is ok occasionally but not for customer-facing chat frequently. Need p95 mostly under 250ms for 512 tokens, like Jared said earlier.
[03:02] Jared Kim: Correct, p95 <= 250ms is our bar.
[03:06] Carlos Ortega: We'll target that in the benchmark. For sizing, I'll need your qps histogram and concurrency percentiles, plus model sizes and quantization tolerance.
[03:16] Lina Zhao: We'll upload traffic trace and model list to the shared folder after this call.
[03:21] Maya Patel: Great. On reserved profiles - we offer 3 options: small reserved pool (cost-efficient), medium (balanced), large (sustained high-throughput SLA). For POC we usually recommend medium to show steady-state performance.
[03:36] Samir Patel: What's the expected cost delta between reserved and on-demand burst?
[03:40] Carlos Ortega: Reserved is roughly 40-60% cheaper per GPU-hour versus on-demand depending on instance type and commitment. But you pay for baseline even if underutilized. Bursting is more expensive per token but only used during short spikes.
[03:52] Jared Kim: OK, want to model costs - show us a cost projection for our traffic shape.
[03:57] Maya Patel: Carlos will produce a spreadsheet with a few scenarios: reserved-only, reserved+burst, and aggressive autoscale.
[04:05] Lina Zhao: On fallback policies - we need guaranteed correctness when we fall back: same API, but possibly a quantized model or an approx-faster model. Can Redwood do automatic reroute and signal to client which variant is used?
[04:18] Carlos Ortega: Yes - we can inject a response header or telemetry flag. Policy options: 1) degrade to quantized variant, 2) route to a cheaper region, 3) return 429 for non-critical requests. We can chain policies.
[04:31] Samir Patel: We prefer automatic degrade to quantized variant first, then region failover if variants saturated. 429 only for non-UI async jobs.
[04:40] Jared Kim: Also how are KV caches shared across variants? We don't want cold KV cache when switching to variant.
[04:46] Carlos Ortega: Good Q - cache compatibility depends on model family and tokenizer. We support cross-variant prefix caching for compatible quantized variants, but not across different architectures. We'll call that out in the sizing sheet.
[04:58] Maya Patel: For benchmarks, propose two phases: Phase 1 - baseline functional test to validate p50/p95 under controlled load, Phase 2 - spike tests to validate burst behavior and fallback policy. Phase 3 - cost sim for 1M token bucket.
[05:12] Lina Zhao: Timeline? We need results before our internal vendor review on April 15.
[05:16] Maya Patel: Tight but doable. Proposed schedule: sizing workbook by April 1, benchmark run April 7 (we'll need an agreed test harness), analysis April 9, proposal April 2 (proposal earlier), final results and decision prep by April 13.
[05:30] Jared Kim: Can you run the benchmark in our VPC or do we need to send data out?
[05:35] Carlos Ortega: For POC we can run in Redwood Dedicated (hosted) with private peering to your VPC, or run entirely in your VPC with Redwood Private. For speed let's start with hosted Dedicated and use VPC peering for secure traffic.
[05:46] Samir Patel: Peering is fine. We'll need the network checklist.
[05:50] Maya Patel: We'll attach the network checklist and security pack.
[05:53] Speaker 2: [inaudible]
[06:00] Carlos Ortega: On metrics to capture: p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, GPU utilization, queue lengths, cold-start counts, billing estimate per token. Also trace-level logs for retries.
[06:12] Lina Zhao: Please include error taxonomy - what counts as degraded vs failed.
[06:16] Carlos Ortega: Yes we'll include an error map.
[06:19] Maya Patel: For the POC reserved capacity recommendation - with your baseline/peak numbers and model mix, my rough call is: reserve 2x A100-equivalent GPUs for the medium profile to cover steady state and autoscale with up to 6 GPUs for burst. That gives coverage for 60-80 qps baseline and up to ~350 in bursts with prewarming.
[06:39] Samir Patel: 2x A100 seems light, but acceptable for a short POC; how do you handle KV cache sharding during scale-out?
[06:46] Carlos Ortega: Our runtime shards KV cache and maintains hot keys on prewarmed workers. During scale-out we replicate KV as needed to new workers; initial tokens may see slightly higher latency until KVs are warmed, which is why we recommend a small prewarm buffer.
[07:00] Jared Kim: What about model quantization - will quality degrade? We need evaluation on prompt sets.
[07:06] Carlos Ortega: We'll include quality regressions in the benchmark: run your eval prompts through the full model and the quantized variant and surface ROUGE/embedding similarity metrics and a small human check set.
[07:18] Lina Zhao: Good. Also need audit logs for every inference at least level-1.
[07:22] Maya Patel: We'll provide audit log options and retention tiers.
[07:26] Samir Patel: On failover to another region, is data residency impacted?
[07:31] Carlos Ortega: Yes, region failover can change residency. We'll include residency guard rails so region failover only happens if you opt in and specify allowed fallback regions.
[07:41] Jared Kim: Ok noted.
[07:44] Maya Patel: Let's talk about SLA in POC - we can commit to monitored SLO targets in the POC but enterprise SLA is part of Dedicated contract. POC will have monitoring and a remediation plan.
[07:55] Lina Zhao: That works. Can you show us cost per million tokens for the different reserved profiles?
[07:59] Carlos Ortega: We'll model that in the spreadsheet. For ballpark, reserved medium might be X per 1M tokens (we'll fill real numbers) vs burst-only could be 2x.
[08:10] Speaker 3: [crosstalk]
[08:15] Maya Patel: For the benchmark harness we'll need an agreed producer: one that replays traces with realistic concurrency and token length distribution. Do you want Redwood to run the harness or do you want to run from your side into our endpoints?
[08:28] Jared Kim: Prefer Redwood to run the initial harness to reduce friction. We'll provide traces and keys.
[08:33] Carlos Ortega: Great. We'll need 3 things: 1) trace, 2) list of models and tolerances, 3) success criteria spreadsheet.
[08:42] Lina Zhao: We'll drop those by EOD tomorrow.
[08:45] Maya Patel: Awesome. On contract terms, POC is typically 4 weeks with a small platform fee and usage billing. Are you ok with a 4-week POC?
[08:55] Jared Kim: Yes 4-week is fine. Our procurement will need statement of work and data processing addendum.
[09:02] Maya Patel: We'll include a DPA and standard SOW template.
[09:06] Samir Patel: For monitoring during the POC can we get token-level telemetry to our Datadog?
[09:12] Carlos Ortega: Yes we have tracing hooks for Datadog, we can instrument the endpoints.
[09:17] Lina Zhao: One more - do you support pinning model versions for rollout testing?
[09:21] Carlos Ortega: Absolutely, we support version pinning and can do canary rollouts and automatic fallback if quality drops.
[09:28] Jared Kim: For the spike behavior what is the maximum safe concurrency per GPU you recommend for the 20B reranker?
[09:34] Carlos Ortega: For a 20B reranker on A100 with quantization and optimized kernels, safe concurrency is 2-4 requests per GPU for low latency; for 7B chat we can push 8-12 depending on prompt length. We'll put exact numbers in the sizing workbook.
[09:47] Maya Patel: We'll also include recommended kernel/compilation flags for your workload.
[09:50] Speaker 1: [inaudible]
[09:55] Carlos Ortega: On billing estimates, we'll create a per-case projection: reserved cost + burst usage per spike profile.
[10:01] Samir Patel: Ok. Are there any hard blockers?
[10:05] Jared Kim: Need to validate data security and residency, and confirm the fallback variants' quality. If both good, procurement ok.
[10:12] Maya Patel: Understood. We'll prioritize security pack and sample quality evals.
[10:16] Lina Zhao: Also please document the failure modes and expected recovery times.
[10:21] Carlos Ortega: We'll add an incident playbook for POC.
[10:24] Maya Patel: Great. Quick recap of owners: Carlos - sizing workbook and benchmark plan; Maya - proposal + SOW + security pack; Lina/Jared - provide traces and success criteria.
[10:37] Jared Kim: Yep.
[10:38] Samir Patel: Thanks all.
[10:40] Maya Patel: We'll schedule the benchmark for April 7, and I'll send the invite after I share the proposal. Thanks everyone.
[10:48] Lina Zhao: thanks.
[10:50] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: minor mis-hearings in a few timestamps, occasional speaker overlap, referenced docs: shared sizing workbook link (to be provided), security pack link (to be provided), benchmark harness script repo (to be provided).
